body: Welcome. Over about ninety days you will get one short note a day to help you make room for fun, silliness and play again.
For now, just notice how often your days are filled with tasks and obligations. There is no need to change anything yet.
Many adults stop playing not by choice but by habit. Seriousness creeps in slowly, and play can return in the same gentle way.
Remember one thing you loved doing as a child purely for fun. Let yourself enjoy the memory for a moment.
Play is not a reward you earn after the work is done. It is part of a full, healthy life in its own right.
Notice any thought that says play is silly or a waste of time. That voice is simply a habit, not the truth.
Laugh at something small today, perhaps a pun, a funny memory or an animal doing something daft. Let the laugh be as big as it wants.
Play is anything you do for its own sake, with no goal attached. It can be quiet, loud, alone or with others.
Notice when you feel most relaxed and light. Those moments often point towards your natural kind of play.
Think of the people in your life who seem playful. What do they do that you might quietly borrow?
Hum or sing along to a song you love while doing a chore. Let it be a little off key.
Being serious does not make you more responsible. Rest and fun actually help you carry responsibility better.
Take a different route on a walk, purely to see what is there. Curiosity is a form of play.
Notice if you feel embarrassed at the idea of being silly. Embarrassment usually fades once you actually start.
Doodle for five minutes without trying to make anything good. Squiggles, spirals and wobbly cats all count.
Play does not need a lot of time. Even two minutes of something light can change the tone of a whole day.
Play a simple game with someone, such as cards, a word game or noughts and crosses. Winning is optional.
Make up a silly name for an everyday object in your home and use it all day without explanation.
What kind of play suits you: physical, creative, social, or puzzles and games? Simply notice what draws you.
Jump in a puddle, kick a pile of leaves or avoid the cracks in the pavement. Let your inner child choose.
You are allowed to enjoy something you are not good at. Being a beginner is part of the fun.
Dance for the length of one song, alone in the kitchen if you like. No one needs to see.
Build something with whatever is to hand, such as a tower of books, a card house or a paper aeroplane.
Notice how your body feels after a moment of play. Lighter shoulders and an easier breath are good signs.
Tell someone a terrible joke on purpose today. Groans and eye rolls count as success.
Play often feels awkward at first because you are out of practice. Keep going and it will loosen.
Put one small playful thing in your diary for this week, like a board game evening or a kickabout in the park.
Try a colouring page, a jigsaw or some modelling clay. Let your hands play while your mind rests.
Work will always expand to fill your time if you let it. Protecting a little play is an act of care.
Arrange your lunch into a funny face before you eat it. Small mischief with food is allowed for grown-ups too.
If you pass a park with swings, have a go. Notice whether a smile arrives before you even notice it.
Laughter is easier with others. Send a friend something funny today, just to make them grin.
Have a go at a pastime you once dismissed as childish. Kites, marbles and hopscotch are all fair game.
Notice the difference between rest and play. Both matter, but play adds a spark that rest alone does not.
Say yes to one playful invitation this week that you might normally turn down.
Write a short silly poem about your morning. Rhymes are optional but strongly encouraged.
You do not need to justify play by calling it productive. Fun for its own sake is reason enough.
Play hide and seek with a child, a pet or even a friend who is game for it.
Try something with a bit of mess in it, like finger painting, baking or digging in the garden soil.
Notice if guilt shows up during play. Thank it for trying to keep you on track, then carry on playing.
Wear something a little bolder or brighter than usual, simply because it makes you smile.
Invent a small game for a boring task, such as racing the kettle to finish the washing up.
Playfulness makes you easier to be around. People often relax when someone else gives them permission to be light.
Blow bubbles, skim stones or fly a paper plane. Simple toys still work their magic on grown-ups.
Put on a funny voice while reading something aloud, whether to yourself, a child or a patient friend.
Look back over the past few weeks of small play. Which moment made you feel most alive?
Spend ten minutes on whichever kind of play you have enjoyed most so far. Follow whatever lights you up.
Learn a game you have never played before. Working out the rules is part of the adventure.
Being silly is not the same as being foolish. It takes a quiet kind of confidence to let yourself be light.
Start a water fight, a pillow fight or a snowball fight if the weather and company allow.
Make up a story with someone, taking turns to add one sentence at a time. Let it get as ridiculous as it likes.
Notice how play changes your mood for the rest of the day. Small sparks often last longer than expected.
Leave a playful note for someone, such as a doodle on a sticky note or a riddle on the fridge.
Seriousness has its place, but it does not need to run every hour. You can switch between modes.
Spend some time outdoors with no plan at all. Wander, poke about and see what catches your eye.
Book a taster session in something playful, like improv, juggling or roller skating. Wobbling is expected.
Put on a song that makes you want to move and let yourself move however you like.
Play can be a shared language. Notice how playful moments bring you closer to the people around you.
Build a den out of blankets and cushions, even for ten minutes. Then sit inside it with a cup of tea.
Notice whether play has started to feel more natural. Practice makes lightness easier to reach.
Gather a few friends for a games night, or suggest one for the coming weeks.
Fold a paper hat or crown and wear it while you do something ordinary, like checking the post.
You are not too old for fun. Age changes the kind of play you choose, not whether you deserve it.
Try to make yourself laugh on purpose, then notice how quickly a fake laugh turns into a real one.
Join in a sport or active game just for fun, without anyone keeping score.
Fun is a skill as well as a feeling. Every small playful act you choose makes it a little stronger.
Ask someone what they did for fun as a child. Their answer might give you a new idea to try.
Create a tiny ritual of play, like a silly dance before work or a daft joke at dinner.
Notice how play helps you cope with stress. Lightness gives your mind more room to think clearly.
Let a playful idea interrupt something serious for a moment. A small giggle will not derail your day.
You are becoming someone who makes room for fun. Notice how that feels compared with when you began.
Plan a playful day out, such as a funfair, a crazy golf course or a beach with buckets and spades.
Play with a pet or a friendly animal if you can. Their joy in the moment is wonderfully catching.
Play is not a break from real life. It is part of real life, as important as work and sleep.
Choose one playful thing to keep doing every week. Make it something easy to protect.
Revisit a game or toy you loved long ago. See whether it still sparks the same delight.
Notice if your old all-work habits try to creep back in. Gently invite play back into the gaps.
Invite someone else to play today, whether that means a kickabout, a puzzle or a daft dance.
Be curious rather than efficient for one small task. Let it take a little longer and enjoy the detour.
Playful people are not careless people. They simply allow joy to sit beside their responsibilities.
Write down three ways you have played over these weeks. Let the list remind you what is possible.
Do something spontaneous with no planning at all, even if it is just skipping down the hallway.
Notice how others respond to the lighter version of you. People often enjoy it more than you expected.
Set aside a small amount of play time each week and write it somewhere you will see it.
Some weeks will be busy and play will shrink. That is fine, as long as you keep inviting it back.
Laugh at a small mistake of your own instead of scolding yourself. Lightness is often the kinder choice.
You now know how to find play in small moments. That skill will stay with you long after these notes.
Today, play the way you most love to play. Let it be a celebration of how far you have come.
Think about what play has given you over these weeks: more laughter, more ease, perhaps closer connections.
Look back at the person who started these notes, so used to being serious. Notice how much lighter you feel now.
Keep a little room for silliness every day. It does not need to be big to make a real difference.
Thank you for these ninety days. Keep playing, keep laughing and let fun stay a natural part of your grown-up life.
